title: Notre Dame’s defense dominates Boston College in blowout win. Here’s what else we learned
content:
SOUTH BEND, Ind. — If anyone needed a reminder about where this season is supposed to go, it was happening over Marcus Freeman’s shoulder as he gave a halftime interview to NBC with Notre Dame already in control against Boston College.

As Freeman talked through how Notre Dame shook off any hangover following the Miami win a week earlier, the Notre Dame Stadium video board played a trailer for “Here Come The Irish,” the program’s in-house docu-series releasing next month. The first audio of the preview? An ESPN talking head cutting straight to the chase: “Everyone is going to remember Notre Dame did not get into the College Football Playoff” last season.

Yes, everyone will remember, including Notre Dame.

Instead of laboring through the game after game, No. 5 Notre Dame blew out Boston College 41-7, taking care of business as the regular season hits its home stretch. The Irish close with SMU and Syracuse before learning where it’s headed next, presumably the CFP.

Here’s what we learned during Notre Dame’s latest demolition job.

Bo MacCormack III is now the answer to a trivia question.

Who was the first running back to score a rushing touchdown against Notre Dame this season, and how long did it take? The Boston College sophomore is the answer after his three-yard touchdown run early in the third quarter. It was the 289th carry the Notre Dame defense faced this season and the first time one crossed the goal line (the Irish had allowed four rushing touchdowns to quarterbacks this season).

Otherwise, Notre Dame’s defense dominated Boston College, although MacCormack capped a modest 27-yard touchdown drive which began after CJ Carr’s interception to open the second half. The Eagles finished with just 136 yards of offense and posted -10 yards in the second quarter, including Boubacar Traore’s strip sack turning into a Jaylen Sneed fumble recovery in the end zone. Traore was a former Boston College verbal commitment. Now he’s a potential All-American for Notre Dame.

It’s hard to know what Boston College’s performance means, considering its offense is built around quarterback Mason McKenzie, a Division II transfer who leads the team in passing and rushing. Point being, Boston College was not constructed to test Notre Dame’s defense.

If not for Carr’s interception and Jordan Faison’s fumbled punt return in the second quarter, Boston College would not have run a play in Notre Dame territory until the fourth quarter.

At a minimum, Notre Dame’s defensive performance felt like an extension of last week when defensive coordinator Chris Ash called a more aggressive game than some of his more reactionary game plans earlier this season. The Irish finished with just two sacks, but they gave McKenzie almost no time to operate. Notre Dame also played without defensive tackles Francis Brewu and Jason Onye. The two suffered knee injuries against Navy and were questionable the past two weeks before being scratched.

No problem.

As Boston College defensive back KP Price threw CJ Carr to the turf early in the fourth quarter, it was hard not to wonder why the Eagles were allowed to touch Notre Dame’s quarterback. Marcus Freeman had already pulled every other offensive starter, including the line tasked with protecting the potential first-round pick. Would another touchdown pass against a woeful ACC program really change Heisman voters’ hearts and minds?

Probably not.

After playing the best game of his college career against Miami, Carr was more than fine against Boston College. He finished 20-of-28 for 217 yards, two touchdowns and one interception, just his second pick of the season. It was respectable work. It’s just not the kind of box score that makes a player lift the Heisman Trophy in New York City.

And that’s fine.

This year’s Heisman race feels more open than most, and Carr does have a good chance to get to New York, probably sitting next to presumptive favorite Jeremiah Smith. The Ohio State receiver posted 11 catches for 117 yards and a touchdown against Northwestern on Saturday, bringing his season stat line to 69 catches, 1,200 yards and 14 touchdowns. He’s posted 100-yard games six times and went over 200 yards in two.

Meanwhile, Carr has just one 300-yard passing game all season, although last year’s winner Fernando Mendoza also had just one 300-yard game for Indiana. Still, unless Carr rewrites some single-game passing records to finish the regular season, it feels safe to assume he won’t be Notre Dame’s first Heisman Trophy winner since Tim Brown in 1987.

Again, that’s fine because Carr is trying to be Notre Dame’s first national championship-winning quarterback since Tony Rice.

It’s a good thing Notre Dame no longer has to worry about making the College Football Playoff after beating No. 1 Miami last weekend because the Irish schedule is shaping up to be as bad as many feared before the season kicked off.

Aside from Boston College offering little resistance, Notre Dame watched Wisconsin lose to listless Maryland while Wake Forest throttled SMU. When the Mustangs come to Notre Dame next weekend, SMU will not only be unranked but also out of sight and out of mind nationally.

That means Notre Dame will finish the regular season having played just two ranked teams: Miami and BYU. And it wouldn’t be a surprise if the Irish end up facing eight teams that finish with a losing record.

Does this matter for Notre Dame’s hunt to win its first national title in 38 years? Only in the sense it might make climbing to No. 4 in the final rankings difficult, which is how high the Irish have to go to get a first-round bye. Win two more games and Notre Dame should secure hosting a first-round home game, which was a fine platform for that run to the national championship game two years ago. And Notre Dame could argue it could be better served by playing in the first round, considering the Irish won’t play on conference championship weekend.

A bye would mean a five-week break between the end of the regular season and the start of the playoffs. A first-round game would still give Notre Dame a three-week break before kicking off the postseason. Teams that played in the first round of the past two CFP’s are 7-1 in the quarterfinals, with Alabama’s loss to Indiana last year in the Rose Bowl the only outlier.

At this point, it feels safe to pencil Notre Dame into the postseason. But as the Irish schedule continues to fall apart, it’s a reminder of how important the Miami win is.
